claim: The family of Shimul Sheikh (35) of Bichhali village, Narail Sadar, alleges that two neighbours, Khairul Islam (33) and Shariful Islam (28), promised that through them he would get a good job and an iqama (work permit) in Saudi Arabia for Tk 5 lakh; the family raised the money by selling a motorcycle, mortgaging land and borrowing at interest, and he went in May 2025.
why_new: A 2025 Saudi case sold by neighbours.

claim: Shimul Sheikh said by video call in September 2025 that he was told he would drive a company vehicle for Tk 70,000 to 80,000 a month and that the company would get him a licence, and that he was later asked for another Tk 1.5 lakh for the licence; according to the family no work was arranged, fresh money was demanded and, because they could not pay, no iqama was made.
why_new: The exact second demand (Tk 1.5 lakh "for the driving licence") after arrival, and no iqama when it was not paid.

claim: Shimul Sheikh's mother said that when the family could not pay again he was held and a man calling from an unknown number said he would be in danger unless money was paid, and that he escaped; in September 2025 he said he was on the run, hungry and had been chased by police the day before.
why_new: Held, family threatened from an unknown number, then undocumented and hiding from police.

claim: Shimul Sheikh's father said a village arbitration with local elders failed because the accused would not accept it; his mother filed a case in a Narail court (the article, published 29 September 2025, prints the date as 22 October), and the court ordered the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) in Jashore to investigate; the PBI sub-inspector said the investigation was continuing.
why_new: Arbitration failed; a court complaint was sent to the PBI. The printed case date is inconsistent with the publication date and needs checking.

claim: The accused Shariful Islam denied the allegations: he said Shimul was given a driving job as agreed but could not drive, was then placed with another company, ran away from it and is working with one of Shariful's cousins, that the iqama was made, and that the claims of a fresh demand for money and threats are false; Khairul Islam was not found at his house.
why_new: The accused's version.

claim: Tanvir Hassan Zoha, prosecutor and special investigating officer at the International Crimes Tribunal, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that fieldwork shows that in many cases a trafficking victim is taken abroad, tortured and a ransom is demanded, and that with quick, coordinated steps it is possible to bring the victim back and arrest the trafficker.
why_new: A prosecutor's statement confirming the torture-for-ransom pattern and that fast action has brought victims back.

claim: Nayem Uddin of Narsingdi went to Malaysia in November 2023 through a broker, spending Tk 5 lakh 20 thousand borrowed at interest; he told Prothom Alo he was promised work in a tiles factory but given construction work for a company, which stopped his work after 15 days, kept him in an office for another two and a half months and then suddenly sent him home, where he could not pay the loan instalments.
target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
why_new: A dated Malaysia case of a different job on arrival ending in forced return.

claim: Md Shanto Khan of Jamira village, Phultala, Khulna, went to Saudi Arabia through a dalal in 2020 at a cost of Tk 4 lakh 20 thousand, on the understanding that he would work as a cleaner in a bank; he said he was first given work at a petrol pump and then in a date garden, and did not get the monthly wage he had been promised.
target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
why_new: A dated, named Saudi case: bank cleaner promised, petrol pump and date garden given.

claim: Shanto Khan fell ill within two years, came home in mid-2023 by what he described as more or less running away, and said in October 2024 that the bank loan his father took and the money borrowed from relatives for the trip were still unpaid.
target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
why_new: How the case ended: return after about three years with the debt unpaid.

claim: Islam Hossain of Dumuria upazila, who told his story at a workshop in Khulna, said that in Oman he was not given the wage and the work he had been promised and was made to work 12 to 15 hours; he stayed five years and came home in 2020 during the Covid pandemic.
target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
why_new: An Oman case; the section has none.

claim: The same worker wrote that the man through whom he went was from the next village, had lived in Saudi Arabia for about five years and was known locally as polite and decent; the man fixed the visa price at Tk 4 lakh and promised work at a good chocolate company, and when the worker's guardian asked him directly whether it was a chocolate factory he said to have faith and not worry.
target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
why_new: What the seller said when asked to confirm the job. The article gives the man a pseudonym.

claim: He wrote that a driver took the group from King Khalid airport in Riyadh to a company room in Malaz, that he bought his own food for a month with no work, and that the man who sent him, who lived far away near the Yemen border, put him off for two months with 'today or tomorrow'; there was no chocolate factory.
target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
why_new: What the first two months looked like.

claim: Saiful Malik, additional superintendent of police (Sadar Circle), Cumilla, said at the roundtable that many people go abroad through dalals without a valid contract and later become undocumented, that complaints include not getting fair work or pay and even being held, and that action is hard to take because the necessary papers are missing.
target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
why_new: A police officer saying cases fail for want of a written contract.

claim: Fatema Akter, a returnee woman worker, told the Cumilla roundtable that she worked in Oman for five years on a salary of only Tk 12,000, then went to Saudi Arabia and worked two years, where she said she received a salary of about Tk 3,000 for some of the time; she said food was not given properly, wages were not paid regularly and she was made to work all the time, and she came home ill.
target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
why_new: A woman's wage figures for Oman and Saudi Arabia. Her wording on the Saudi pay is unclear (monthly or total) and is given as printed.

claim: The Attorney General, Md Ruhul Quddus Kajal, told reporters on 4 October 2026 that Bangladesh's labour market in Malaysia collapsed because of money taken beyond the fixed fees, people promised one job and given another, and fake visas, and that cases were filed during the interim government against those involved and charge sheets submitted after investigation.
target_section: Contract substitution: a different job or wage on arrival
why_new: The state's chief law officer names job substitution and fake visas, with overcharging, as the grounds of the Malaysia cases; the section has no Malaysia entry.

claim: Marina Sultana, director (programme) of RMMRU, said at the roundtable that research shows about 31% of people who go abroad are cheated in one way or another, and that fraud happens at different steps starting from the passport.
target_section: Dalal scams: the usual tricks and how to spot them
why_new: A headline fraud rate for the Dalal scams chapter's "In one minute"; she does not name the study, so the source needs finding.

claim: Professor Tasneem Siddiqui, executive director of RMMRU (the Refugee and Migratory Movements Research Unit), said on 30 July 2026, citing a study by the organisation, that about 51% of migrants are cheated in one way or another, 19% paid and still could not go abroad, and 32% were tortured after going abroad.
target_section: Dalal scams: the usual tricks and how to spot them
why_new: Three prevalence figures from RMMRU; the 19% who paid and never went belongs in "Refund refusals after a failed departure". The article gives no year or sample for the study.

claim: The Bangladesh High Commission in the Maldives warned in its notice of 22 May 2024 that there is no scope to work in the country outside the approved employer, and said a number of unskilled workers had been sent home for breaking this law.
target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
why_new: An earlier dated warning, with the fact that deportations had already happened.

claim: The same worker wrote from Riyadh in August 2025 that dalal rings bring workers from Bangladesh through various agencies on false promises but cannot give them work, so many have to hunt for work themselves; he said he had seen cheated workers sleeping on the street and one preparing to kill himself under the weight of debt.
target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
why_new: An eyewitness account from inside Saudi Arabia.

claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that workers who spend BDT 4 to 7 lakh on a Qatar "free visa" find on arrival that there is no assured job for them: a company's name is on the papers but in reality there is no work.
target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
why_new: The section says free-visa workers find no job; it does not say that the visa papers still carry a company name that has no work behind it.

claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that in practice a "free visa" means sending a worker without any specific job, and that the arrangement is a form of visa trading from which brokers, recruiting agencies and some dishonest businessmen profit.
target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
why_new: Names who profits (brokers, recruiting agencies, some businessmen), attributed to a named migration researcher.

claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that in Doha and the areas around it countless Bangladeshi workers now wait for temporary work, some get no work for weeks on end, and many go unpaid for months.
target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
why_new: Ground-level detail on what joblessness in Qatar looks like (waiting for casual work around Doha, weeks without work); the section only says they hunt for illegal day labour.

claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that thousands of Bangladeshi workers in Qatar are now without work or pay, that a large share of them are jobless after being cheated through visa trading and broker rings, that some have become undocumented and that many lack food and medical care.
target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
why_new: A dated (May 2026) expert statement on the scale and condition of jobless Bangladeshis in Qatar; the author gives no count beyond 'thousands'.

claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that after the 2022 football World Cup ended, employment fell in a large part of Qatar's construction sector, many companies wound up their projects and many laid off workers, so new job openings are fewer than before.
target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
why_new: Explains why a Qatar free-visa holder now finds no work: the post-World Cup fall in construction jobs. The section has no such explanation.

claim: Qatar's labour minister, Dr Ali bin Samikh Al Marri, said during his visit to Dhaka that began on 17 May 2026 that about 4 lakh 73 thousand Bangladeshis work in Qatar and about 30 percent of them work on development projects, according to a Prothom Alo column of 26 May 2026.
target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
why_new: The section's numbers have no figure for how many Bangladeshis work in Qatar.

claim: According to data from the overseas employment ministry, as cited in a Prothom Alo column of 26 May 2026, 1 lakh 7 thousand 598 workers went from Bangladesh to Qatar in 2023.
target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
why_new: Annual outflow to Qatar; not in the section.

claim: At the seventh Bangladesh-Qatar joint committee meeting on 18 May 2026 Qatar showed interest in recruiting technical workers, especially electricians, plumbers, welders and AC technicians, and its labour minister said Qatar wants to take skilled workers directly from five specific Technical Training Centres (TTCs) in Bangladesh, according to a Prothom Alo column of 26 May 2026.
target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
placement: other: what Qatar says it is hiring
why_new: Sets what Qatar officially asked for (named skilled trades, direct from five TTCs) against the no-job 'free visa'; the column does not name the five TTCs.

claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that it must be ensured that no worker can go abroad without a contract for a specific job, and that sending workers in the name of a "free visa" or uncertain employment must stop.
target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
why_new: A warning quoted from a named expert, which the spec asks for.

claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that Qatar free-visa workers who find no job go around looking for day labour or temporary work illegally and many are at risk of police harassment, arrest or being sent home.
target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
why_new: The section already states this; the draft supplies the Prothom Alo quote and date in case the existing sentence needs a second source.

claim: Amnesty International's documentation says migrant workers in Saudi Arabia have been cheated by recruitment brokers, forced to work extra hours and had wages stolen, in some cases probably amounting to trafficking for labour exploitation; IOM lists irregular migration, hidden work such as domestic, sea or informal work, undue employer control, recruitment corruption and dependence on third-party brokers among the risk factors for migrants in Saudi Arabia.
target_section: Free visas and visa trading in the Gulf
why_new: Named-organisation statement on Saudi recruitment abuse; weak but usable context.

claim: The additional deputy commissioner said that among the complaints from migrants that reach the Deputy Commissioner's office, embezzlement of money sent from abroad and family disputes are prominent, and that a person abroad cannot protect his family and property.
why_new: Remittance embezzlement at home as a leading complaint; no section covers it, so this placement is approximate.

claim: Ali Akbar Khan, acting additional inspector general of police at the CID, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that the biggest challenge in investigating human trafficking is collecting information and evidence across countries and identifying technology-based money transactions, and that investigating cryptocurrency, hundi and online transactions needs modern software, training and international cooperation.
why_new: The CID itself says trafficking payments through hundi, cryptocurrency and online transfers are hard for it to trace.

claim: Dipta Rakshit, Bangladesh country representative of Winrock International and director of its Ashshash project, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that the channels used to move money, including bKash, Nagad, hundi and cryptocurrency, must be effectively monitored and held accountable, and that the flow of human trafficking money must be brought under strict watch.
placement: other: NGO statement on payment channels
why_new: Names the payment channels (bKash, Nagad, hundi, cryptocurrency) an anti-trafficking NGO says carry trafficking money.

claim: Two of the five signs of a fake UAE job offer named by MOHRE in November 2026 are being told to open a new bank account in your own name as part of recruitment, and being asked to receive money into your bank account or move it from there to another account.
why_new: Bears on the section's open question about job seekers' accounts being used to move other people's money: an official warning that fake job offers ask for exactly this.

claim: Marina Sultana, director (programme) of RMMRU, told a Prothom Alo and Democracy International roundtable in Cumilla on 11 April 2026 that 31 percent of the people who go abroad are cheated, which she attributed to the lack of a law for the intermediaries or sub-agents.
why_new: A headline share of migrants cheated, from a named researcher; target is the In one minute of the Dalal scams chapter. Her "no law" premise conflicts with the guide (sub-agent registration has been in the Act since 2023); see the next draft.

claim: The five Sherpur, Bogura, men who paid Abdul Alim for work abroad said some of them had borrowed and some had sold land and cattle to raise the money.
why_new: How the money for a failed Malaysia departure was raised.

claim: Md Selim of Narayanganj, who went to Malaysia in March 2023, did not get the promised job and paid his own fare home in September 2023, told Prothom Alo he had sold his own auto-rickshaw and his wife's jewellery and borrowed from people to go, and was now destitute and in debt.
why_new: The guide uses Selim's job and injury; this adds how he financed the trip and the dates.

claim: In a Prothom Alo video cited in a 4 June 2024 column, Mohammad Kolim from Barishal, standing on the airport road, said he had paid with a loan taken at interest and could not go to Malaysia, and Belal Hossain from Cox's Bazar said part of his money came from his father, part from uncles who mortgaged the homestead and part from selling cattle, and that all of it was lost.
why_new: How two of the stranded workers had raised the money.

claim: A study published on 18 February 2025 by IIED (the International Institute for Environment and Development), based on a survey of 648 households in 33 villages of Mathbaria, Pirojpur, and Gowainghat, Sylhet, found that a family spends Tk 4 lakh 61 thousand 220 in Pirojpur and Tk 4 lakh 13 thousand 667 in Sylhet to send a member abroad, raised by selling land or by high-interest loans, and that the migrants are not aware of their rights and so are easily cheated.
why_new: District-level cost-of-migration figures for 2025 and how the money is raised; the section has national figures only.

claim: The IIED study said people who migrate abroad are more helpless than internal migrants because they borrow to go and it is almost impossible for them to come home without repaying the loan, and that with the distance, the cost of travel and the wish to provide for the family they bear everything in silence.
why_new: Explains why the debt keeps a worker in a bad job abroad; the section lists borrowing but not this effect.

claim: The IIED study found that climate risk raised the likelihood of households in the surveyed areas of Pirojpur and Sylhet migrating abroad by 214 percent (against 161 percent for moving to another town inside Bangladesh), that most of those going abroad go to the Gulf countries, and that a third of them work as construction labourers in risky conditions.
why_new: Who is being pushed abroad and into which work; a driver the guide does not mention.

claim: Shakirul Islam, chairman of OKUP (Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program), who was involved in the IIED study, told Prothom Alo in March 2025 that when disasters leave people no alternative work locally the decision to migrate is taken by the family and at least one member leaves in search of work, but there is no arrangement to protect these migrants.
why_new: Named expert on migration as a family decision under distress.

claim: Abdullah Rubel of Padmapukur union, Shyamnagar, Satkhira, mortgaged his family's shrimp farm for a loan and went to Brunei in 2019; he found no work there, did all the household work in a Bangladeshi's home in return for food and lodging with no wages, and after nine months borrowed again to buy a ticket home.
why_new: A Brunei no-job case financed by mortgaging the family business.

claim: Abdullah Rubel told Prothom Alo in March 2025 that he had spent Tk 5 lakh to go abroad and still had not been able to repay the loan and recover the shrimp farm.
why_new: Six years on, the mortgaged asset is still not recovered.

claim: A study by OKUP and the International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED), 'Exposed and Exploited: Climate Change, Migration and Modern Slavery in Bangladesh', surveyed 648 households in 33 villages of Mathbaria, Pirojpur, and Gowainghat, Sylhet; it found people from Mathbaria who migrated abroad spent Tk 4 lakh 61 thousand 220 on average, raising 25% of the money by selling land and 18% from high-interest loans.
why_new: A local average cost and how it was financed (land sale 25%, high-interest loans 18%).

claim: The OKUP and IIED study says that people who go abroad on borrowed money are forced to accept any work, and found that 99% of the workers had faced at least one sign of modern slavery (low wages, withheld wages, physical and mental abuse, restrictions on movement) and 81% more than five.
why_new: Links the debt to what the worker has to accept abroad, with survey figures.

claim: Afaz Uddin said the BDT 24 lakh he paid in 2024 for a promised Canada job was all his savings plus loans from acquaintances and relatives, and his wife said the family was still paying interest on the money they borrowed.
why_new: Debt left behind by an online scam.

claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 21 February 2026, citing the paper's own report, says an 18-year-old from Chandanaish, Chattogram, who hoped to go to South Africa, was sent abroad on a Tk 9 lakh loan that was beyond his family's means, and that his journey ended in his death in a foreign land.
why_new: A South Africa case; the guide has no South Africa route. The editorial gives no date, place or cause of death, so the underlying news report should be found before use.

claim: Prothom Alo reported in May 2026 that Arif Hossain of Santoshpur, Sandwip, was cheated after going to Saudi Arabia and had to return home after only 27 days, and Arif said he had sold his electronics shop to get the visa and now has nothing left.
why_new: A dated case of a business sold for a visa and a return within 27 days (the article does not say how he was cheated).

claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza of North South University's Centre for Migration Studies wrote that he learned from talking to many Bangladeshi workers in Qatar that to go there some sold land, some borrowed at high interest and some left their families in debt, and separately that a large share of workers went abroad on loans and, without regular work, cannot send money to their families at home.
why_new: A Qatar example of land sale and high-interest borrowing for a visa with no job; based on the author's own conversations with workers, no names or counts given.

claim: IOM's Farzana Shahnaz said in May 2026 that people often go abroad at high cost on borrowed money and their income is almost used up repaying the loan, so a person needs to understand beforehand what going will cost, what they will earn, how long they will stay and what gain is left at the end.
why_new: A named IOM officer confirming that earnings go on loan repayment; the section has this from a former secretary only.

claim: Abdullah Al Zobayer (24) of Mirsarai, Chattogram, told Prothom Alo in June 2024 that he trusted a friend who was the younger brother of a Libya-based broker and a member of the ring, was taken to Libya on the promise of Italy, and that the ring collected BDT 4 lakh from his family.
why_new: The recruiter was the victim's own friend; the section lists standing and track record but not friendship.

claim: Local people in Bhairab, Kishoreganj, said in July 2024 that several broker rings sending people to Italy by sea through Libya had been active there for 10 years and that many people did reach Italy through them; the most active, Rasel Mia's ring, then took several crore taka from 24 people, none of whom reached Italy.
why_new: Adds to 'People he has already sent': a ten-year local track record, followed by a batch of 24 none of whom arrived.

claim: The man arrested in the Shariatpur case, Rashed Khan of Charjadabpur village, Shariatpur Sadar, works at sending manpower to various countries and has a firm named Lamisa Enterprise, according to police and relatives; one wife said her husband left home with him on 3 February 2024.
why_new: A broker with a named firm and a known manpower business in the district; the article gives no licence.

claim: Ashek Elahi alleged that on 14 December 2023 a group attacked his house and forcibly took his mother's signature on four blank bank cheques and 20 blank non-judicial stamp papers, that on 17 March 2024 Tarek Aziz's father took his uncle's signature on five blank stamp papers, that his family filed a court case to recover them, and that the cheques and stamps were then used to file the trafficking case against him.
why_new: The guide says only that the accused claimed his signature was taken by force; this gives his detailed claim about blank cheques and stamp papers and the counter-case.

claim: The August 2026 explainer said a fraudster calls on WhatsApp or imo from a number with Canada's country code (+1), and that anyone outside Canada can make a call from a Canadian country-code number online.
placement: other: new item (A foreign phone number)
why_new: A foreign country code is not proof the caller is abroad (the June 2026 CID case shows the same with an Australian number on imo).

claim: Kawsar Khan wrote on 20 August 2026 that fraud rings usually pick Australian visa categories such as Working Holiday (subclass 417) or eVisitor (subclass 651), whose list of eligible countries does not include Bangladesh: they enter an eligible country in the online application to get a quick digital visa, then use the facility for correcting details to add the applicant's Bangladeshi passport number.
placement: other: new item (A visa that shows online)
why_new: The exact mechanism by which a real Australian government check comes to show a 'granted' visa against a Bangladeshi passport.

claim: As a result, Kawsar Khan wrote, the government's preliminary checking system shows the visa as granted, but in reality it is impossible to travel directly on that visa; people he warns answer 'but the visa is showing online!'.
placement: other: new item (A visa that shows online)
why_new: An online 'granted' result on the official system is not proof.

claim: Kawsar Khan wrote in August 2026 that the biggest bait of Australia visa fraudsters is 'visa first, money later' (আগে ভিসা, পরে টাকা).
placement: other: "Pay the balance after the visa."
why_new: Confirms from an immigration lawyer that 'pay after the visa' is itself the bait, alongside the section's two cases.

claim: According to the UN commission, the Russia job offers seemed credible to recruits because of the recruiters' assurances, their own earlier experience of working abroad, information from others who said they had got the same work, and documents showing the recruiting firm's government approval; in some cases an acquaintance had told them about the job.
why_new: A UN finding on what made the offer believable, including the firm's government approval papers.

claim: A Bangladeshi worker in Riyadh wrote in August 2025 that he learned only after reaching Saudi Arabia that his visa had passed through the hands of six dalals before it reached him, that he had had no way of knowing this while in Bangladesh, and that after he found no work in Saudi Arabia he spoke to five dalals.
target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
why_new: A worker's own count of the chain (six hands), matching the TIB figure with a first-hand account.

claim: Jesia Khatun, director of WARBE Development Foundation, said at the roundtable that because recruiting agencies are concentrated in Dhaka, dalals play the important role in the field; Farzana Alam Majumder, a BAIRA member from Cumilla, said the problems seen most are unlicensed dalals, false promises, cash transactions, fraud and keeping the contract paper hidden.
target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
placement: other: why dalals fill the gap
why_new: An agency-side speaker naming "keeping the contract hidden" and cash dealing as the commonest problems.

claim: Md Nazmus Sakib, assistant director of the District Employment and Manpower Office in Sylhet, said on 18 April 2026 that about 2,900 licensed agencies send workers abroad but all are Dhaka-centred, that only a few agencies work directly in Sylhet and the rest work as brokers under the cover of travel agencies, and that money beyond the set limit is being taken as a result.
target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
why_new: A DEMO official saying that outside Dhaka the 'agency' a migrant meets is usually a travel agency acting as broker.

claim: Mohammad Nasir Uddin, general secretary of the Sylhet District Press Club, said on 18 April 2026 that Sylhet has over 150 licensed travel agencies but more than 500 agencies are in fact active illegally, taking BDT 8 lakh to 20 lakh to send people abroad (he gave no source for the figures).
target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
why_new: A local estimate of unlicensed travel agencies in Sylhet and what they charge; unsourced, attribute to the speaker.

claim: Ariful Haque Chowdhury MP, the Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that Dubai is taking 6 thousand drivers and that the ministry is arranging for its representatives to come to Bangladesh and recruit workers directly once they are satisfied with the training, which he said would leave middlemen no scope for fraud.
target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
placement: other: a recruitment channel without middlemen
why_new: A specific demand (6,000 drivers for Dubai) and a direct-recruitment arrangement announced by the minister in August 2026; the article gives no detail on how to apply.

claim: Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC's Migration Programme and Youth Platform, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that recruiting agencies are Dhaka-centred, that there is no agency in Sylhet, Tangail, Munshiganj or the other districts from which most people go abroad, and that people there are connected to Dhaka through middlemen; because of these middlemen at home and abroad and workers' lack of skills, he said, Bangladeshi workers' cost of going abroad is the highest in the world and their income comparatively low.
target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
placement: other: why the village needs a middleman
why_new: Explains the root of the chain: no agencies in the high-migration districts (three named), so the link to Dhaka is the middleman. The section describes the layers but not why they exist.

claim: Ali Haider Chowdhury, former secretary general of BAIRA, told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that dependence on brokers would fall if the list of legal recruiting agencies and correct information about jobs reached upazila level.
target_section: The chain from the village to the visa seller
why_new: A former BAIRA official conceding that agency lists and job information do not reach upazila level; a recommendation, not an existing service.

claim: Iqbal Mahmud, deputy team leader at The Asia Foundation, told a Prothom Alo roundtable in Cumilla published on 30 April 2026 that the 2023 amendment to the overseas employment law spoke of regularising dalals and rules were made in January 2025, but that in practice there has been little progress in registering dalals and bringing their work inside a structure.
placement: other: answers the Need to know on registration
why_new: Bears directly on the section's open question "Has BMET registered any sub-agents yet": as of April 2026 a named practitioner says little progress.

claim: Iqbal Mahmud said the recruiting agency completes the visa process but collecting workers and other important work is done through dalals; Kamruzzaman, principal of the Cumilla Technical Training Centre, said a clear decision is needed on which body (the ministry, BMET or another) regulates sub-agents and middlemen, and that with no defined structure they often take advantage.
why_new: A government training-centre head saying it is unclear who regulates sub-agents.

claim: The IIED study lists the seizure of migrants' visas and passports abroad, withheld wages, forced work, restriction of movement, threats and beatings, and excessive or unpaid work among the practices it counts as modern slavery.
target_section: The passport kept by the dalal
why_new: A research source classing passport seizure abroad as modern slavery.

claim: The CID said in September 2025 that the Josna Khatun ring, which took money for jobs abroad and gave fake visas, also held on to many victims' passports to harass them.
target_section: The passport kept by the dalal
why_new: Another dated case of passports held as a lever.

claim: Naznin Akter, a Bangladeshi woman who returned from Malaysia, told a roundtable on technology-driven fraud and human trafficking held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 22 July 2026 that on arrival in Malaysia on 15 November 2025 her passport, ticket and papers were taken from her and she was told there would be no work until the balance was paid.
target_section: The passport kept by the dalal
why_new: A case of the passport (and return ticket) being seized abroad as leverage for more money; the section's cases are in Bangladesh and Cambodia.

claim: After the special mobile court at Triple A Overseas (RL-2630) on 10 September 2026, led by a BMET executive magistrate on the minister's instruction, the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry said the three boxes of passports taken irregularly from Malaysia-bound workers were in BMET's custody, and that returning them to their real owners through legal process and taking legal action against the agency were under way.
target_section: The passport kept by the dalal
why_new: The guide has the raid, fine and seizure; it does not say where the passports went (BMET custody) or that owners are to get them back through a legal process. The article does not say how an owner claims one.

claim: Several BAIRA members allege that part of each Malaysia worker's cost in 2022-24 went to Ruhul Amin, known as Swapan, and part of that was laundered to Malaysia through hundi, with the rest going to the agency in whose name the worker was sent, and that in every case the money changed hands in cash without any receipt; Ruhul Amin told Prothom Alo the allegations were false, that nothing was taken beyond the government-fixed Tk 78,990 and that no money was sent to Malaysia.
target_section: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts
why_new: Cash-without-receipt applied even between agencies, with the accused's denial.

claim: At a BRAC Migration Programme workshop in Khulna on 31 October 2024, attended by Khulna's additional deputy commissioner, a Khulna Metropolitan Police deputy commissioner and chaired by the assistant director of the Khulna manpower and employment office, speakers said migrants are cheated most when they go through brokers, that many keep no proof of the money they hand over when going abroad, and advised keeping proof of every transaction.
target_section: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts
why_new: Advice from officials at a named event that matches the section; adds a 2024 source.

claim: The worker wrote that he borrowed the Tk 4 lakh from relatives and paid the agency in instalments, sometimes Tk 50,000 and sometimes Tk 1 lakh, and that when he went to the agency's office in Dhaka to collect his papers before the flight he was treated very badly and the agency took more money from him on various pretexts.
target_section: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts
why_new: Extra money taken at the agency office on the day of the flight, after the full price was paid.

claim: The Minister for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, Ariful Haque Chowdhury, said at a roundtable in Sylhet on 18 April 2026 that the government is building a system to stop people being cheated by paying brokers, and plans, in discussion with the Bangladesh Bank governor, to introduce a 'Probashi card' so that migrants are served through a set system instead of cash transactions.
target_section: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts
why_new: A stated government plan (not yet a scheme) to replace cash payments; the guide has nothing on it.

claim: Police said the Nilphamari ring arrested in July 2026 took money in stages by mobile banking under the heads of medical fee, visa processing fee, document verification, ticket and other incidental costs, after assuring people the job abroad was confirmed.
target_section: The staged-payment trap, and no receipts
why_new: Adds 'medical fee' and 'ticket' to the fee labels, from a police account.

claim: Cumilla City Corporation's administrator said some training centres have irregularities: training is given but a proper certificate is not, and employment is promised but does not happen.
why_new: A local official on training centres that promise jobs.

claim: Nu-Emong Marma Mong, deputy manager (overseas recruitment) of BOESL, said in May 2026 that BOESL has sent women workers to Jordan's garment sector entirely free of cost since 2010, with its officers handling everything from the medical and pre-departure training to getting to the airport, and that BOESL tells workers the fixed migration cost for each country in advance.
why_new: BOESL's own statement that the Jordan garment channel is wholly free, including the medical and training, since 2010; supports the section's red flag with what the free channel covers.

claim: BOESL's deputy manager described its process: it starts with a government-to-government agreement or an employer giving BOESL the recruitment, labour wing officers at the Bangladesh embassy verify the employer's demand, the information is then published as a notice and a test is held with the employer or its local representative present, and BOESL helps with all the legal steps of going abroad after the test.
why_new: The genuine sequence of a BOESL recruitment (verified demand, public notice, test with the employer present), against which a fake "BOESL" offer can be checked.

claim: The ILO's Rahnuma Salam Khan said an assessment of 40 technical training centres (TTCs) found that the training at TTCs under BMET is in many cases not fully in line with the demand of labour markets abroad.
why_new: An assessment finding on government training centres; context for why workers go unskilled.

claim: On 30 July 2026 the state minister for expatriates' welfare, Md Nurul Haque, asked how agencies take Tk 12 to 15 lakh from a person going to Singapore, and said the Singapore authority does not take that money: six training institutes have been authorised, they charge, and by doing business as a syndicate they are becoming owners of hundreds of crores of taka.
why_new: The section covers Saudi and Jordan only; this is the Singapore training-centre route, with a price (Tk 12-15 lakh) and the number of authorised centres (six), from the state minister. He does not name the six.

claim: On Friday 9 October 2026 the Special Response Battalion (SRB-4) arrested 12 members of a ring at Technical Mor, Dhaka, accused of taking money on promises of jobs abroad, working visas and a guaranteed pass in the written test; a mobile court then sentenced seven of them to between seven days and three months in jail and fined five.
why_new: Possibly the same raid as the section's '9 Oct 2026, 20 arrested in Shyamoli' case from another source: this report gives 12 arrested at Technical Mor, the unit (SRB-4) and the sentences; reconcile before adding.

claim: SRB said the ring arrested on 9 October 2026 guaranteed people wanting to go abroad a worker visa at low cost and a pass in the written test, took between BDT 40,000 and BDT 10 lakh from candidates depending on the case, and then kept the money on various excuses.
why_new: The price range (BDT 40,000 to 10 lakh) for a 'guaranteed pass'.

claim: According to the SRB press conference of 9 October 2026, BOESL's test is held every Friday and Saturday at the venue of the Bangladesh-Korea Technical Training Centre (BKTTC), and the broker ring worked mainly by targeting the candidates who gathered there for the test.
why_new: Where and when the brokers find their targets: outside the exam venue on exam days.

claim: The SRB press conference said BOESL, under the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, recruits workers for abroad on the government's behalf, takes no fee from candidates in the recruitment process, and that a person with only a passport can get overseas work through the test at no cost.
why_new: As stated by SRB; compare with the guide's wording that BOESL takes a fee only after final selection by pay order.

claim: SRB-4's commander, Lieutenant Colonel Hafizur Rahman, said BKTTC is a training centre teaching 24 trades in courses of various lengths, that its certificates help in getting a job abroad, but that it does not send workers or arrange jobs, so taking training and getting a job are not the same thing.
why_new: A training centre's name is used to sell jobs; the centre sends no one.

claim: The 9 October 2026 action began with complaints from BKTTC and BOESL, after which SRB ran a shadow investigation and raided with an executive magistrate present; SRB asked anyone cheated in this way to inform the authorities quickly and to verify information through government offices and approved agencies.
why_new: How the enforcement was triggered (the institutions themselves complained) and the mobile-court route.

claim: The worker wrote that he later learned his visa belonged to a 'supply company' (a labour-supply firm) and that the villa he was housed in belonged to the same company; by his description, a supply company sells workers on to other places at a high price for its own profit, and the worker placed there is not paid.
why_new: The "supply company" visa, a term and mechanism the section does not have: the worker is hired out by the visa holder rather than left to find work.

claim: A Prothom Alo editorial of 24 October 2025 says that under ILO conventions there is no such thing as a free visa: it is a fraudulent arrangement in which the worker is only given permission to enter a country, or a sponsorship is sold, with no specific job arranged.
why_new: The guide cites BMET for "no such thing as a free visa"; this adds the ILO framing as stated by the newspaper. The OKUP survey figures in the editorial (five times the set cost, 72% loans, 11% mortgage, 6% asset sales, 43% no work, 7% through agencies) are already in the guide.

claim: The same column puts the cost of that Saudi job at about Tk 5 lakh 70 thousand: about Tk 4 lakh 60 thousand taken by the recruiting agency as its fee, about Tk 60,000 more for the passport, medical test, Takamol certificate, PDO training and police clearance, and roughly Tk 50,000 paid to sub-agents at various levels.
target_section: What people pay, and to whom
why_new: A three-way split (agency, papers, sub-agents) for a Saudi job; the section has a split only for a Cambodia case. It is a columnist's estimate, not a survey.

claim: Md Atikur Rahman, assistant director of the Cumilla District Employment and Manpower Office, said at the roundtable that agencies do not fully follow the policy and in many cases take extra money from unskilled or uneducated people.
target_section: What people pay, and to whom
why_new: A DEMO official admitting agencies overcharge.

claim: Mahbubul Mannan Chowdhury, acting regional head of Probashi Kallyan Bank (PKB, the state bank for migrants) in Sylhet, said on 18 April 2026 that by the ministry's list going abroad through the government channel costs about BDT 1 lakh 60 to 70 thousand, but that most people in practice spend more than BDT 4 to 5 lakh, and that agencies' profit reaching BDT 2.5 to 3 lakh cannot be justified.
target_section: What people pay, and to whom
why_new: A PKB regional head's figure for the gap between official cost and what borrowers actually pay, and his estimate of the agency margin.

claim: Studies of Bangladeshi workers in the Maldives by RMMRU with the Asia Foundation found that 96 percent of the workers who went there had gone through relatives or dalals, that irregular workers work for lower pay, and that a legal worker sends home more than Tk 3 lakh a year against more than Tk 2 lakh for an irregular one, Prothom Alo reported in May 2024.
why_new: A corridor-specific share of dalal or relative recruitment and the earnings gap for irregular workers.

claim: The Prothom Alo guide of 7 July 2025 said dalals usually press people by saying they will get the work done quickly, do not show proper papers and hide their own identity, and deceive with false visas, job offers and demands for extra money.
why_new: A published list of dalal behaviours; unattributed newspaper advice, so weaker than a case.

claim: The column says there are very few legal recruiting agencies in the Rangpur region, so people there cannot even learn how going abroad works, and names lack of agencies, lack of a migrant network, inability to raise several lakh taka and fear of dalal fraud among the reasons few people go abroad from Rangpur division.
why_new: Regional gap in licensed agencies; low priority.

claim: At the same roundtable the administrator of Cumilla City Corporation, Md Yusuf Molla, said most people who are cheated abroad are cheated because of the persons who act as intermediaries, and that Bangladesh has no law for intermediaries in the migration process and needs one at once.
placement: other: what officials believe (conflicts with the guide)
why_new: Evidence that local officials in a high-migration district did not know of the 2023 sub-agent provisions the guide describes; not to be stated as fact.

claim: Farzana Alam Majumdar, a sub-agent and member of BAIRA, told the Cumilla roundtable that the main problems in the sub-agent and recruitment system are false promises, cheating in cash transactions and keeping the contract hidden, and recommended that BMET bring all sub-agents under registration and that the ministry frame rules for the system.
why_new: A working sub-agent naming the three main abuses, including hiding the contract, and saying in April 2026 that sub-agents still need to be registered.

claim: Cumilla's additional deputy commissioner (general) Md Saiful Islam said in April 2026 that migrants have long demanded a one-stop service, and that people choose dalals because the government has not yet managed to provide it and the dalal or intermediary provides that service.
why_new: An official's own explanation of what the dalal sells: the one-stop service the state lacks.

claim: Md Saiful Islam, additional deputy commissioner of Cumilla, said that because the government has not fully started a one-stop service many people turn to dalals, who handle the whole process of sending a person abroad from start to finish, and that the person often does not know how or at what cost he is going.
why_new: A district official on why the dalal wins: he does everything in one place.

claim: In a Prothom Alo column published on 26 May 2026, Dr Selim Reza, associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies at North South University, wrote that many people, from village-level middlemen to licensed recruiting agencies, are part of the broker ring that controls Bangladesh's overseas employment sector, and that overcharging workers, false promises, fake contract papers and supplying illegal visas have become a "normal" business process.
placement: other: expert statement on the chain
why_new: A named researcher's statement that licensed agencies, not only village brokers, are part of the chain; opinion, to be used as an attributed statement.

claim: Rahnuma Salam Khan, senior national programme manager of the ILO, said in May 2026 that the government clearly set out in a 2025 set of rules what the responsibility and accountability of recruiting agencies and sub-agents will be, but that effective implementation or enforcement of these rules has not yet begun.
why_new: Answers part of the section's Need to know: as of May 2026 the 2025 licence and sub-agent rules were not being applied, according to the ILO.

claim: Marina Sultana, programme director of RMMRU, said in May 2026 that RMMRU helped the government frame the rules that later provided in law for the registration of sub-agents, but that this has still not been fully implemented, and that it also worked on alternative dispute resolution so that BMET's arbitration process becomes more transparent.
why_new: A second named source that sub-agent registration was not fully implemented by May 2026.

claim: Sheikh Romana, general secretary of the Bangladesh Ovibashi Mohila Sramik Association (an association of women migrant workers), said in May 2026 that of about 2,200 agencies 1,100 are valid, and that ethical recruitment has still not become real.
why_new: A count of agencies and how many are valid, from a workers' association leader; unsourced by her, so to be checked against BMET's licence list.

claim: Farzana Shahnaz, a national programme officer of IOM, said in May 2026 that for lack of correct and reliable information people at village level depend on dalals for information, and that a pilot initiative funded by the Italian government has been taken to deliver information through Union Digital Centres (UDCs, the government's grassroots-level service centres).
why_new: Names an alternative information point at union level (UDC pilot); the article does not say in which unions.

claim: Md Badrul Haque, administrator of BAIRA (the Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies), told a roundtable on safe migration and the reintegration of returnees held at the Prothom Alo office in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 that not all recruiting businessmen are dishonest and many send workers following the rules, while some fraud rings spread their nets in remote areas and take people's money.
why_new: The recruiting agencies' association's own position on fraud rings; generic, usable only as an attributed statement.

claim: RMMRU says India has 192 recruiting agencies, Pakistan 464, Nepal 416 and Sri Lanka 248, while Bangladesh, which once had 850 to 900, was taken to nearly 2,400 under the last Awami League government; the interim government approved 252 new licences in 2025 and 2,646 agencies in all have taken licences, Prothom Alo reported on 5 September 2026.
why_new: The number of licensed agencies against neighbours'; RMMRU's point is that fewer agencies are easier to monitor.

claim: Dr Selim Reza wrote on 9 September 2026 that recent studies show a large share of people waiting to go abroad have not finished secondary education and most rely on relatives, local brokers, sub-agents and informal networks instead of licensed recruiting agencies, adding that these are indications of a trend, not exact national statistics; by government figures, he wrote, 8 to 9 lakh of the roughly 22 to 23 lakh young people entering the labour market each year have to look for work abroad.
why_new: Context figures; low priority, since the section already has survey percentages for broker use. The studies are not named.
